As the scholar al-Qushji says, the image is in the shared inner sense. There is a difference between actually seeing something and imagining it, and there is no doubt that the state described here is one of seeing.

A Persian verse arranges the parts of the eye in this order: the hard outer coat, the choroid, the retina, the vitreous fluid, the crystalline fluid, the arachnoid layer, the albuminous fluid, the iris, the cornea, and the joining layer. The traditional anatomy described here divides the eye into seven coats and three fluids. The hard coat begins at the end of the tough membrane around the hollow optic nerve. Anatomists say there are two membranes inside the skull around the brain, one thick and one thin, as well as an outer membrane covering the skull.

The choroid is described as woven from the ends of the thin membrane and from veins and arteries. It is compared to the placenta because of its many vessels, or because it forms a net around the eye's contents. The retina is said to begin at the ends of the hollow optic nerve. It surrounds the vitreous and crystalline fluids and extends to the arachnoid layer, like a net holding a catch. Others say its name comes from the many vessels that pass through it from the thin membrane.

The vitreous fluid is described as clear, thick, and slightly reddish, like melted glass. It surrounds the back half of the crystalline fluid and feeds it. Since the crystalline fluid is very white, clear, and bright, the account says it cannot be made directly from blood; the vitreous fluid serves as an intermediary. It is clear because it feeds what is clear, reddish because it comes from blood, and thick so that it does not leak away. It lies behind the crystalline fluid because its supply comes from the brain through the retina, and so it must connect to it and lie closer to its source of nourishment.

The crystalline fluid, also called the icy fluid, is described as clear and firm like ice. It is the eye's most important part, where sight occurs; the other parts serve and protect it. It is placed in the center because of its importance and is compared to a mirror in which images form. The arachnoid layer is said to be extremely thin, like a spider's web, and to cover the front of the crystalline fluid. It begins at the retina and separates the crystalline fluid from the albuminous fluid, which is excess nourishment. Constant contact with this excess would be harmful, so the layer is thin enough not to block light or images from reaching the crystalline fluid.

The albuminous fluid is described as resembling egg white in color, clarity, and thickness. It lies in front of the crystalline fluid to soften strong light before it reaches it, keep it moist so air does not dry it out, and protect it from the roughness of the iris. The iris is described as a thick layer, hard on the outside and soft and sponge-like on the inside. Its central opening faces the crystalline fluid and lets light through, like the hole left when a grape is pulled from its stem. The iris also holds the albuminous fluid in place and keeps debris from reaching the pupil. Aristotle is said to have considered the eye's natural color black, because black gathers and strengthens sight and moderates light. Galen is said to have favored blue, arguing that black compresses the visual spirit too much while blue, with its whiteness, spreads it out and strengthens sight. The note adds that Aristotle supposedly had dark eyes and Galen very blue ones.

The cornea is described as a hard, clear layer like white horn thinned by scraping. It begins at the hard outer coat and protects the layers and fluids beneath it. It is said to have four layers, like horn, so that if one is damaged, the others still protect the eye. It is clear so that light can pass through, like the glass of a lantern that protects the flame without blocking its light. The joining layer is described as a firm, clear, cartilage-like covering, connected to muscles and containing soft white tissue that lubricates the eye and eyelid and keeps them from drying out as they move. Hippocrates is said to trace it to the outer membrane over the skull, while Rufus traces it to the inner tough membrane. Unlike the other layers, it joins around the cornea rather than covering it; the note says that this is why it is called the joining layer. The account says these details are stated in medical works.
The front of the crystalline fluid is slightly flattened. At the back, it extends lengthwise so that it can fit into the hollow optic nerve.

It is better to say that these images are present in the shared inner sense. That sense receives images both from the outer senses and from inner imagination, as happens in sleep and similar states. Usually, the outer senses occupy it and prevent images from within from appearing. This obstacle is removed in sleep, when the outer senses weaken, or when they are deliberately weakened. The intellect's use of imagination for matters that are not sensed is another obstacle; illness can remove it. In some conditions affecting the brain, the first obstacle also falls away, either because the bodily vital spirit is too weak or scant to spread outward or because inner images become unusually strong. Once both obstacles are gone, the shared sense sees the images imagination creates, and imagination then retains them. The inner powers are like mirrors facing one another; the shared sense is like a two-sided mirror, facing outward and inward. The note adds that the answer in the main text may also mean that proof of how sight works in one case does not by itself establish how it works in every case.

The argument is not strong against this view. Someone who says that the second image seen by a person with crossed eyes, or an image in a mirror, exists in the imaginal world can also say that the images seen by people with certain illnesses exist there and are present to them.

On this account, visible objects that have images in matter are present directly to the soul with all their features: shape, position, direction, distance, and so on. The images seen by people with certain illnesses are in their own souls and arise from them, so they are present to them even more clearly. The first claim is hard for many people to accept, but the second should be clearer.
The claim that sight happens at once, without comparison or inference, is disputed. Careful experiments and investigation point the other way.
The author of The Discussions objects because the distinction between something with no size and something that can take on any size has been overlooked.

One can object that this argument is disproved by clear water, crystal, and similar things: they have no color, yet images appear in them. The reply is that, although the crystalline fluid has no color, it has a substance or thickness like water, unlike air. Anything with substance and a distinct form can receive an image. This means that the author's praise of the next two arguments as strong applies only to the last one.

The first argument assumes, without proof, that whatever color reaches the eye remains pure. The second says that what someone sees in another person's crystalline fluid is not the visual image by which sight itself occurs. This has been established, so both arguments apply only against those who say that an image is imprinted in the crystalline fluid.

First, it is not established that a physical body can act on a distant body only after acting on every nearer one. The sun warms and lights things here, but does not do the same to things nearer to itself.
In the author's view, all these factors still play a part by preparing the conditions for sight.
This is a fair statement. But the author should allow the same point to those who support imprinting, since their claim does not conflict with the soul being the one that perceives.

One might object that the angles and the circle become smaller, but the visible object does not shrink. Why not let the base of the cone cover only part of the object, so we see that part and then mistake the whole for something small? The reply is that on the ray view, the base of the cone is where sight occurs. At a distance it works like a small mirror: the whole object appears in it, but small. On the imprint view, the object's image is imprinted in a small area of the crystalline fluid, forming an imagined cone whose point is at the center of the fluid and whose base is the object. As the object moves farther away, the angle narrows and the part of the fluid receiving its image becomes smaller, so the image is smaller too. On the ray view, a distant object also looks less clear because the ray weakens as it travels farther from its source.

In air, the visible object does not stay large because the cone narrows as the object gets farther away. In water, the rays gather together, so the image looks like it is in a larger mirror and the object appears larger.

One might object that rays and water are both simple, with similar parts, so all the rays should either travel straight or bend in the same way. The reply is that the ray along the axis is stronger. Differences in strength could explain why some rays travel straight and others bend.

The point is that after shutting and reopening the eyes, at first we may see the moon—or any other object—as two, as if one image were pulling away from the other. The main text gives only a brief account.

The fingers are not placed on the eyes in different positions; they are placed on one eye in a way that changes its position. The finger presses the eyelid inward and pushes the eyeball outward, changing its usual arrangement.

The wording is sound; it simply leaves out “in the sky” in the first part. In the second, the scholars say that we see a moon in the sky, not in the water. Their view is that rays reflect from the mirror toward the visible object, forming an angle there. When the viewer faces a polished surface, the ray from their sight reflects from it toward the viewer, who sees themself rather than an image or likeness. Because they do not notice the reflection, they think they see themself directly.
Many scholars give this explanation. But if it were right, we should hear one sound as two, since we have two ear canals, unless something brings the sound together as one.
The ray theorists' point would work if it were established that a person with one crossed eye does not see one object as two. The note's author says he has not verified this.

This is a good explanation of how sight might work, but it is not the only possible one. The same arrangement could be explained by rays entering the eye from the visible object rather than leaving the eye and traveling toward it.

These two explanations are weak. First, if we deliberately cross our eyes, or look at two aligned sticks at different distances and focus on one of them, the visual spirit would have to be both moving and still at the same time, or moving in two opposite states. Second, the explanations could lead us to see more than two images, as when a lamp is reflected many times in rippling water.

Here, “indirectly related” means related through something else, in a loose sense. Strictly speaking, an indirect relation is only a figure of speech and cannot prove the point. The argument also falls short because it assumes that a physical effect must take place outside the body that causes it. That is not established; forms can act on the matter and bodies that receive them. Nor has it shown that the affected body must be separate from the cause. The claim that two connected bodies act like one is an analogy, not a proof. This question should be settled by observation, not by reasoning alone.

The size that allows a natural body to be divided, whether by actual cuts or in thought, is an essential feature of that body, not a feature that exists separately from it. The arrangement of a body's parts, set by how they relate to one another, is part of how the body exists and what makes it the body it is. “Position” can mean a simple relation to something else, such as being beside or facing it. It can also mean the arrangement of a body's parts in relation to one another and to what surrounds it, as when a person stands upright. If the parts keep the same arrangement but their relation to the surroundings changes, the first kind of position changes but the second does not. The author means this second kind of position: the body's own arrangement, which is part of its existence. Even if he also means an outside relation, such as nearness, the reasoning can still be followed: making an effect depends on existence, and a body's existence depends on an arrangement that connects it with what surrounds it, so its effect also requires a suitable outside relation, such as nearness.

“Position is a way the body exists” means that position is one part of what determines the body's identity. Some philosophers also say that visible, measurable shape is a stage in the existence of a natural body. The idea becomes clearer on that view.

One might object that if being very close makes contact, sight should occur even more easily when the object is extremely close. Why then must a transparent medium lie between them? The reply is that each kind of effect requires a certain arrangement: the object must not be too close or too far, and the connection must run through a transparent medium.

The three possibilities match the three views of sight. The first is the ray view, in which light travels from its source to what it lights. The second is the view that rays leave the eye and reach the object. The third is the imprint view, in which an image travels from the object to the eye.

The argument is well formed, but one of its starting points is only assumed: that human beings are the most complete animals among all living things. Earlier philosophers based their account of creation on the natural sciences and astronomy of their time. They believed that all living animals lived on the earth. Of the kinds they had examined and tested, they regarded humans, with reason and thought as well as animal senses, as the most complete. On that basis, they concluded that humans are the most complete animals known to us. If we accept modern scientific ideas that life might exist elsewhere, it is hard to prove that no other animal could be more complete than humans. We would need a separate argument to show that no such animal could exist.

On the common view, the argument is incomplete because something may be possible in itself without being able to occur in practice. It works if “possible” here means possible in the natural world. It also works on the view that everything possible in itself exists in the world of intellect, where it needs no material preparation; intellect can then bring about what lies below it.

On the view being discussed, these might instead be called shared things sensed indirectly, since the five senses are said to sense only qualities. Size, position, and similar features would then not be directly sensed. The author replies that these features themselves affect the sense and are present to it. We sense them in their own right, not merely because they accompany another sensible quality. They are not indirect just because another feature helps us recognize them.

The source passage is not fully clear. The note's likely meaning is that each sense has its own proper object, while shared features—such as distance or shape—can be perceived through more than one sense and with help from thought.

Direction is a shared feature that all the senses can perceive. Even taste can tell whether a flavor comes from outside the mouth or from the throat. It is harder to say that senses other than sight and touch perceive size directly.
This refers to where something is. Taste senses qualities such as flavor strongly, but senses where something is only weakly.

This is why some philosophers found bodily resurrection difficult and turned to the idea of transmigration. In the author’s view, the front part of the brain is where common sense appears, not where it resides. Calling it a power of the soul means that it belongs to the soul, not the body. Saying that it is prepared to arise in the brain means that the soul’s power is disposed to act there, not that the power itself is physically located there. The soul is likewise prepared to be connected with the body, but is not physically situated in it.

An objection: the one who judges must have both things being compared, and the relation between them, present to the mind. Since that relation is a meaning perceived by estimation, this argument does not prove common sense. The reply is that relations among images are themselves image-like, just as relations among meanings are conceptual. The sky’s being above the earth is a relation of position; the soul’s being above its powers is a conceptual relation. Common sense perceives the first, while estimation perceives the second when it concerns a particular thing.

I say that the argument is strong. Matter and form, though both kinds of substance, are not a body by themselves. Their combination becomes one, forming a new kind of thing: a body. In the same way, the whiteness we see and the sweetness we taste do not by themselves ground the judgment that “this sugar is sweet.” Nor is their real combination enough. Combining things is the work of a power that acts, not one that perceives—just as wood can join one thing to another without being aware that it has done so. The judgment itself is the perception of the real combination. Judgment is a kind of knowledge: perceiving that a relation does or does not hold. This particular judgment, the perception of how these qualities come together, belongs to common sense, not to intellect at its higher level, since intellect does not perceive or judge particulars there. Even if intellect does perceive particulars, it does so at its lower level, the level of the senses. The power that judges particulars at that level is common sense. If intellect perceived particular sensible things at its higher level, there would be no need for the senses.

I say this is not a real combination or identity, but a unity of another kind. It does not require a separate power. For example, Zayd is a limited, material instance of human nature, while the universal human nature is immaterial. How can one simply be the other, as if they were both particulars or both universals? Their relation is more like that of a trace to its reality. A material thing and an immaterial thing do not form one natural kind, so there is no need for a separate power that unites them. The spiritual heart is enough. In mystical terminology, the heart is the substance that perceives both general ideas and particular things.

The point is that intellect can judge between particulars even though it does not perceive them directly. But the same objection raised against the author applies: if the judge does not perceive particular images, how can it judge? If it perceives them through bodily powers and organs, but is unaware of what those organs perceive, how can it judge then? And if their images are reflected onto the intellect itself, how can they be imprinted on something immaterial? If that is possible, why would the senses be needed?
Bahmanyār’s “another power” means another power in relation to taste and sight, not a power separate from the soul. It would be clearer to say “a different power.”

Even if it does not follow that the two things being judged must be perceived without any intermediary, a particular judgment cannot take place without common sense. I think Bahmanyār means common sense by “another power,” and by denying perception he means denying direct perception.
The moving drop occupies one position after another; the point seen as a line is spread across those positions.

There is no difference between the past or future being separated from the present by centuries or by a few seconds. If sight could perceive these absent things, it could perceive them all, since they are equally absent.

There is an easier argument than the one given by the author: if common sense did not exist, imagination would not be possible. Imagination’s work is to preserve the forms of the five senses. Common sense perceives them in imagination, while imagination preserves them. Each power has its own role, just as each natural power has a distinct role. For example, common sense perceives the image of a speaking or nonspeaking animal; imagination preserves the image and the perception of it.
The phrase is vocalized with two ḍamma vowels.

The name is shared with the formative power found in plants. One might say that “formative” should describe common sense, since common sense perceives and imagination forms. But common sense is like a mirror with two faces, one turned outward and one inward. Imagination forms the inward face.

The point is to prove in general that the powers differ: if one were identical with the other, no case could arise in which one worked without the other. The example of water is not the point of the argument. So the objection that it is only an example does not apply. This proof establishes difference because one power can work without the other; the next two arguments establish it because the powers do opposite things. These are the grounds for distinguishing powers.
The Imam objects that imagination also receives an image before preserving it. The answer is that receiving an image in imagination means forming it there.
This objection concerns the main claim, not the argument for it. The proof rests on the fact that opposing functions cannot belong to the same power in the same way.

I say this objection can be answered: something can be preserved without being judged or accepted. The active intellect, for example, can preserve false ideas without accepting them as true. This is like the distinction between receiving and preserving. Why does the objection work in the first case but not the second?

I think this argument is weak. If imagining means preserving an image, then it repeats the first argument. If it means arranging or perceiving images, it proves the imaginative or estimative power, not the power of imagination that preserves them. A better proof is recollection: we may sense an image and later remember that it is the same image we sensed before. To judge that they are the same, the image must have been preserved in a stable place—namely, imagination.

The source meant here may be the imaginal world, the soul impressed on the celestial sphere, or the imaginal forms and the Trumpet mentioned in scripture. It does not mean God or the active intellect, since immaterial beings are not places where particular imagined forms are stored.

The established habit is an effect of imagination. If “the source that gives images” means this habit, there is no disagreement. If it means an external source, that is not right, since our own experience tells us the habit is within us. Immediate perception as a present act differs from the stable ability to recall something. The first belongs to common sense; the second to imagination.

I have already said that the imaginative power’s work is to act, as when it joins or arranges things without perceiving them. So its work requires the things to be present, but not perceived. Tusi’s reply in effect denies that this work falls under the rule that a judge must have both things before it. This is an act of arranging, not a judgment that a relation holds.

The objector calls using a power an act of that power. If a power acts through an instrument, then the instrument itself must be used by another instrument, and so on without end. Yet no intermediate power is required if the instrument is a sense faculty. It is unlikely that “instrument” here means the vital spirit or bodily organs. The correct reply is that perception and action are one here: estimation’s acting on images is itself how it perceives them. The same applies at each higher level in relation to the lower. The soul uses and perceives its powers, and its perception of them is the same as using them, since it knows them directly. Just as God’s knowledge is His power, the soul’s knowledge of its powers is their use.
The yellow thing may not really be honey. Estimation makes the mistaken judgment that it is honey. When the thing really is honey, the correct judgment belongs to common sense.
Estimation is the ruler of all the animal powers, and the imaginative power, which is its instrument, works in both the front and rear parts of the brain.

If this argument worked, it would show that estimation is intellect restricted to particular things. But it does not. Affection, one of the things estimation perceives, is not merely an abstract relation with no individual instances, nor is it a general kind that has only one instance. There are many particular affections: a person’s love for a child, an animal’s love for its young, or a donkey’s attachment to something. One person may love a child, a spouse, and many other things; a thousand distinct affections may arise in a single day. These inclinations, longings, and affections are particular meanings that exist in the soul: they were not there, then came to be, and later pass away.

A particular meaning of this kind must be perceived in relation to what it is about. The outer senses, common sense, and imagination cannot perceive it, since they perceive and preserve images, while affection and hostility are meanings. Intellect cannot perceive them either, since it perceives universals, while these are particular experiences. Their particularity is not merely a matter of being related to something. So there must be a power besides sense, imagination, and intellect. This is what philosophers mean by estimation. Intellect sees no difference in kind between whiteness and affection as general kinds that can have many instances. The difference is that whiteness has particular visible instances, while affection has particular inwardly experienced instances. The same goes for hostility, dislike, and similar feelings.

The author’s reasoning depends on two claims. First, affection and hostility have no true particular instances of their own; they are only general relations attached to particular images. This is not so. In his discussion of will and aversion in Theology, he himself says that will and aversion are psychic qualities, like other mental qualities, and are known inwardly, like pleasure and pain. Their particular instances are easy to recognize. He adds that perceiving particular instances of each is linked to perceiving particular instances of other things.

Second, the argument assumes that animals without reason perceive particular meanings that are only relations by having their imagination connect with the governing forms of their kinds. Since they have no intellect, their estimation would then be intellect restricted to particulars. If this idea were meant to deny that evil has a real existence—some philosophers say evil is only incidental in the divine order—it should be limited to mistaken estimation, such as wrongly judging that a yellow object is honey or being afraid of a dead person. It should not be extended to a trained dog’s estimation, a parent’s love, trust, or fear of a dangerous enemy.

If the reason for not treating these meanings as a separate realm is that they are not distinct from the images imagination perceives, that would be an arbitrary rule. One could just as well say they belong to a lower spiritual realm, since they are particular meanings in souls connected to spiritual and physical forms, or to a higher realm because of their nobility. I suspect the author was driven by his deep commitment to unity. Since inward meanings do not have the many visible forms, positions, places, and directions found in physical images, it was easier to treat them as one. Yet their subjects and times still differ. Strikingly, the author says this in several places, including The Keys to the Unseen.

There are obvious problems here. The intellect’s recognition of a meaning does not require another power to perceive its opposite. Sight and touch often make mistakes, and the intellect judges that what they perceive is false. Nor do we accept that hostility must be sensed if it is present in an individual. We do not sense bodyhood, unity, or existence with any of the five senses; the senses perceive only a body’s qualities. The author’s proof may be weak, but there is another way to question whether estimation is a separate power. Sensible things are perceived by common sense after they have first been present to the outer senses, such as sight, hearing, and touch. The soul knows these things directly through a kind of union with the bodily powers. In the same way, our ordinary, representational knowledge of inner meanings such as affection and hostility may be preceded by the soul’s direct awareness of them. Why could common sense not perceive these inner qualities, just as it perceives external qualities? The fact that they are called meanings, in contrast to images, because qualities such as heat and blackness can belong to things outside the soul and body, does not prove that they require another independent power. Consider this carefully. If common sense is enough to perceive meanings, then imagination may also be enough to preserve them, and there may be no need for a separate memory power.

Affection, hostility, and similar states belong to the soul, not the body. The soul itself is a particular meaning, which estimation perceives in a general way; this will be discussed when the author treats the soul’s immateriality.

After saying that estimation perceives general meanings attached to images, the author clarifies that he means meanings the mind draws from particulars, such as causality, not qualities such as blackness. For the sake of consistency, however, he should have said that the second kind is perceived either by intellect alone or by one of the senses.
There is room to object to this. Our experience suggests otherwise: it is hard to imagine voluntary actions in animals without a judgment, and judgment requires estimation or intellect.

“The soul is all the powers” does not mean that the soul is merely their sum, since a sum has no separate existence or unity. It does not mean that two things become one, or that the soul leaves one level to take on another. Rather, the soul is the source that remains present at every level: the spirit behind spirits and the form behind forms. It does not leave its higher level when it takes on the features of a lower one, nor does it leave its lower level behind when it develops into a more complete one. This happens through the soul’s own development and change in its being. It has many powers in one, and one soul through many powers. Its existence is one, though the ideas we form from its different levels are not all the same.

This is also an argument from what we know. What we know is something we want or value, and the one who judges must have both sides before them. But if the one who knows what is desirable were not also the one moved to want it, knowledge would not give rise to desire, and desire would not give rise to knowledge. That is not so. So the one who knows and the one who desires are one.
The ideas we draw from the soul’s powers are not all the same. Each action has its own name and meaning.

One might say that this third argument adds nothing, since it is obvious that the soul perceives sensible things. I reply that the argument is not about ordinary, image-based perception. Many people think that this perception belongs to the body’s organs, not the soul. But direct awareness of the body and its powers does belong to the soul. It must happen without an instrument; otherwise, another instrument would be needed to perceive the first one, and the process would never end. So one soul, in different states, perceives both particular things and general ideas.

This can be challenged. The argument assumes, without proof, that the body cannot be a place for desire or anger. Another factor might prevent a desire or anger from arising in a particular part of the body.

The argument shows that desire and anger are immaterial powers, but not by itself that they are the soul. They could belong to another immaterial power. I say the conclusion does follow: a material power would not belong to the soul, but an immaterial power does, since the soul has material, imaginal, and intellectual levels.
This objection is fair. The claim assumes that the brain’s vital spirit has no more capacity to hold images than any other body, but there is no proof of that.
If the imagined size is an immaterial, imaginal form, and imagination is one with what it imagines, then this already proves that imagination is immaterial at the imaginal level.
If Avicenna allowed that the soul creates an image rather than receiving an imprint, this conclusion would not follow. The soul is also immaterial at the imaginal level.

This is based on Avicenna’s rejection of change in a thing’s essence and of the soul’s becoming one with intellect after first becoming one with sense. He does not reject the claim that existence is real in the world or that it can become stronger and weaker.

This applies especially to the vital spirit. If a body or bodily thing could perceive, it would be the most likely place for perception, since the powers are said to exist in it as qualities or forms. The vital spirit is finer than the rest of the body, breaks down more quickly, and needs more replacement. That is why doctors try to strengthen and restore it through food and medicine.

There is another possibility: one image could be formed in the original part only. The author does not mention it because a new part would have to take the place of one that broke down, and the replacement should have the same form as what it replaces.

“Separate sources” here means the soul that is spread through the heavens. Separate intellects cannot contain particular images. Since the author means the soul in the heavens, he raises the question only about the soul.

The text may originally have read: “Just as when the soul gains the ability to connect with intellect, it can recover images from the active intellect after they fade, so it can do the same here.” The copies I have seen read as printed.
A copy made in 1211 AH reads: “When the soul gains the ability to connect with intellect, and the images fade, it can recover them from the active intellect.”

There is no problem on the right account. At the imaginal level, the soul is immaterial in a way that allows it to take on imaginal forms. The difficulty is how these images are made present to the soul, not how they are physically lodged in it.
The words “although it is” should be removed from the sentence.

People may think general ideas come from the heart or brain because they meet them clothed in words and sensible images. Words are sounds made by the lungs and mouth; images, even of touchable things, appear in the head. This can make it seem as if general ideas are located in the heart or brain. But general ideas are immaterial. When a person understands one, the immaterial self takes in all its outward and inward instances. No pine-shaped heart, sticky brain, or bodily spirit could do this.

The individual parts of the body do not truly hear, see, or speak as a person does. “The whole” here means the physical body, which many people think is the human being. Jami’s Golden Chain jokes about this common view: it defines a human as an upright animal with broad nails, bare skin, and no hair. Anyone who looks like that is then assumed to be human.

Even someone who believes that images are physically imprinted can answer this objection. Position and place may belong to the image’s existence without belonging to its definition. The fire imagined in the mind does not burn, and imagining a straight line does not make the mind straight.

The author’s wording is surprising. Mental existence includes both imagined forms and intellectual ideas; both are called what they are in a basic sense, not in the ordinary sense. A mental sphere is not an ordinary material sphere. It is an imaginal or intellectual form.

The stronger reply is like the earlier one about a general sphere. A general square, and the general ideas of right and left, are not right or left in the ordinary sense. If the right and left are particular, the mind is not simply choosing their position; a choice that conflicts with reality would be false. The author does not use the distinction between these two ways of saying “square,” though it appears often in his books, and the people making the argument have missed it.
This refers to “not made of matter.”
The forms made by the soul are the source from which the heavenly spheres come.
Calling the knowledge of higher, immaterial sources “conceptions” is not exact. Their knowledge is direct; it is not made up of ideas and judgments in the ordinary sense.

There is no matter here to receive a new form, as wax receives the shape of a square. Giving an image a specific identity is not a second act added to its creation. The defining feature follows from the image itself.
This is like the forms of the afterlife, which do not have the place and position found in this world.
